Understand DynamoDB from first principles: NoSQL data model, partition/sort keys, Query vs Scan, indexes, consistency, capacity modes, transactions, TTL, Streams, DAX, global tables, and how to answer practical system-design questions.
Amazon DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database. It supports key-value and document data models and is designed for predictable single-digit millisecond performance at large scale.
No servers, database instances, patching, or storage provisioning to manage.
Automatically partitions data and scales storage.
Supports on-demand and provisioned throughput modes.
Integrates naturally with Lambda, API Gateway, IAM, Streams, Global Tables, and DAX.
Unlike an RDBMS, DynamoDB does not provide SQL-style JOIN operations.
A DynamoDB table contains items, and each item contains attributes.
Items in the same table may have different non-key attributes.
Only primary-key and secondary-index key attributes need to follow the declared key schema.
Maximum item size is 400 KB, including attribute names and values.
Do not store large images/videos in DynamoDB. Store the object in S3 and keep the S3 key/URL plus metadata in DynamoDB.
The primary key uniquely identifies an item. Composite keys also let related items be sorted together.
4. What Does the Partition Key Do?
DynamoDB hashes the partition-key value to distribute items across physical storage partitions.
A good partition key has many distinct values and spreads reads/writes evenly.
Poor example for a huge workload: status = ACTIVE/INACTIVE, because most traffic can concentrate on very few values.

A hot partition happens when too much traffic concentrates on a small set of partition-key values. Good key design is the first defense; adaptive capacity helps but does not remove all per-partition constraints.
Items with the same partition-key value can have different sort-key values.
Within a partition key, DynamoDB stores results in sort-key order.
Useful for one-to-many data such as customer -> orders, device -> readings, user -> posts.
Useful operators include equality, comparison/range conditions, and begins_with.
PK = CUSTOMER#123, SK = ORDER#2026-09-29#9001. Query the customer partition and use sort-key conditions to fetch only a time range or item type.
DynamoDB modeling normally starts with the questions your application must answer.
Get all orders for customer X.
Get orders for customer X during a date range.
Find all orders with a given status.
Get products by category and price.
In an RDBMS you often normalize first and query later. In DynamoDB you identify access patterns first, then design keys and indexes so those access patterns are efficient.
Query is targeted. Scan reads the entire table or index before optional filtering.
Admin jobs, migrations, rare broad reads
FilterExpression does not make a Scan cheap. DynamoDB reads items first, then filters the returned results.
Read one item by its complete primary key
Create or fully replace an item
Modify selected attributes; supports atomic counters and expressions
Delete one item by primary key
Read items sharing a partition-key value
Conditional writes make a write succeed only if a condition is true.
Create only if an item does not already exist.
Decrease stock only if stock >= requested quantity.
Condition expressions let DynamoDB enforce concurrency/business preconditions atomically, preventing many read-then-write race conditions.
Store a version attribute in the item.
Client reads item with version N.
Client updates using condition version = N and writes version N+1.
If another writer changed it first, the condition fails and the application can retry/reconcile.
Optimistic locking is useful when concurrent writers might overwrite each other but pessimistic database locking is not available or desirable.
11. Global Secondary Index (GSI) vs Local Secondary Index (LSI)
GSIs are much more common because they allow a completely different query key and can be added later.
Must be same as base table
Required and differs from table sort key
Separate from table for provisioned mode
Requirement: 'Show all PENDING orders for a customer.'
Create GSI with PK = customerId and SK = status#createdAt.
Query customerId and use a sort-key prefix/range.
Create an index because you have a real access pattern. Too many indexes increase storage and write cost because writes must maintain index entries.
A GSI only contains items that have the GSI key attributes.
This can intentionally create a sparse index.
Example: only failed orders contain escalationStatus = FAILED.
GSI PK = escalationStatus gives a small index containing only items needing attention.
Sparse indexes can make rare-condition queries cheaper and faster than indexing every item.
Choose strong consistency only where stale reads are unacceptable.
Eventually consistent reads are the default.
Strongly consistent reads return the latest committed value.
Strong reads are supported for tables and LSIs.
GSI reads are always eventually consistent.
Eventually consistent reads consume half the read capacity of strong reads for the same item size.
A profile page can often tolerate eventual consistency. A just-updated critical balance/state may require stronger concurrency design or a strongly consistent table read.
Most new/interview projects can start with on-demand unless traffic is predictable and provisioned economics matter.
Use when predictability/cost control justifies it
1 RCU = one strongly consistent read/sec for an item up to 4 KB.
1 RCU = two eventually consistent reads/sec for an item up to 4 KB.
1 WCU = one write/sec for an item up to 1 KB.
Larger items round up to the next capacity-unit size.
Transactional reads/writes consume twice the corresponding units.
A 6 KB strongly consistent read requires 2 RCUs. A 1.5 KB write requires 2 WCUs.
Provisioned requests can throttle when available capacity is exceeded.
On-demand can also throttle when table/account/request scaling limits or configured maximum throughput are exceeded.
Poor partition-key distribution can create hot keys/partitions.
DynamoDB provides burst and adaptive capacity to help uneven workloads, but key design still matters.
Use exponential backoff/retry behavior provided by AWS SDKs and monitor throttling metrics.
A physical partition is designed for up to 3,000 read units/sec and 1,000 write units/sec. Avoid concentrating very high traffic on one logical key.
DynamoDB supports ACID transactions for multi-item all-or-nothing operations.
TransactWriteItems supports Put, Update, Delete, and ConditionCheck actions.
Up to 100 unique items can participate in a transaction.
Aggregate transaction item size cannot exceed 4 MB.
All items/tables in a transaction must be in the same AWS account and Region.
Transactions cost more capacity than non-transactional operations.
Use transactions when several related changes truly must commit or fail together, such as order state + inventory reservation + ledger item. Do not use them by default for every write.
TTL lets each item contain an expiration timestamp in Unix epoch seconds.
DynamoDB automatically deletes expired items, typically within a few days after expiry.
TTL deletion does not consume write throughput in the Region where the expiry deletion occurs.
Expired items may still appear in reads until physically deleted, so applications can filter them when necessary.
Good use cases: sessions, temporary tokens, old events, transient cache-like records.
TTL is asynchronous cleanup, not an exact scheduler. Do not rely on an item disappearing at the exact expiry second.
Streams turn table changes into near-real-time events.
Records INSERT, MODIFY, and REMOVE events.
Can include keys, old image, new image, or both depending on stream view type.
Stream records are retained for up to 24 hours.
Use cases: audit workflows, notifications, search indexing, materialized views, downstream synchronization.
DynamoDB Streams preserves modification order for each individual item. Do not assume a single total ordering across all table items.
DAX is an in-memory cache designed specifically for DynamoDB.
A cache hit can provide microsecond response times.
Best for read-heavy, eventually consistent workloads with repeated reads.
On a cache miss, DAX reads from DynamoDB and caches the result.
DAX is not useful if most reads are unique or if the workload requires strongly consistent reads.
DAX is DynamoDB-specific and API-compatible for supported operations. ElastiCache is a general-purpose Redis/Valkey/Memcached cache that your application manages explicitly.
TTL, DAX, and Global Tables each address a different problem.
Global Tables replicate DynamoDB data across multiple AWS Regions.
Multi-active: applications can read and write in replica Regions.
Useful for global low-latency applications and multi-Region availability.
Traditional/default mode is Multi-Region Eventual Consistency (MREC).
AWS added Multi-Region Strong Consistency (MRSC) as a newer option for eligible designs.

MREC favors lower write latency and asynchronously replicates changes. MRSC synchronously replicates before successful writes and supports strong reads across replicas, with different restrictions and higher latency tradeoffs.

Choose DynamoDB when access patterns are known and you need massive scale, low operational overhead, and predictable key-based performance. Choose RDS when relationships, joins, ad-hoc SQL, and relational constraints are central.
Single-table design stores multiple entity types in one DynamoDB table using carefully designed partition and sort keys.
Example PK = CUSTOMER#123, with SK values PROFILE, ORDER#001, ORDER#002.
This can retrieve related entities with one Query.
It reduces joins by colocating data needed by an access pattern.
It is powerful but adds modeling complexity; you do not need to force every small project into one table.

Understand the idea and why it exists. For a 3-YOE full-stack interview, explaining partition/sort keys, access patterns, GSIs, and Query vs Scan clearly is usually more important than mastering every single-table pattern.
API Gateway receives the HTTP request.
Lambda validates the request and uses an IAM execution role.
GSI supports alternate lookup such as customerId + createdAt.
DynamoDB Stream invokes another Lambda for notifications/search indexing.
TTL removes temporary idempotency/session records where appropriate.
The access patterns are known, traffic can spike, and the application benefits from serverless scaling without managing database instances.
Scenario: Need to fetch a user by userId millions of times/day.
Use userId as a high-cardinality partition key; GetItem provides direct key lookup.
Scenario: Need all orders for one customer sorted by date.
Use customerId as partition key and createdAt/orderId as sort key, or design a GSI for that access pattern.
Scenario: Need to find orders by status but status is not part of base key.

Scenario: Writes are throttling on one celebrity user key.

Scenario: A just-written value must be immediately read as latest from the base table.
Use a strongly consistent table read if the design requires it.
Scenario: Need strong read from a GSI.
Not supported; redesign to read the base table/LSI or change the access pattern.
Scenario: Need session records deleted after 24 hours.

Scenario: Need to run logic whenever an item changes.
Enable DynamoDB Streams and consume with Lambda.
Scenario: Need atomic update of order + inventory reservation.

Scenario: Read-heavy product catalog needs extremely low latency.

DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL key-value and document database. It automatically manages storage, partitioning, availability, and scaling and is designed for predictable low-latency access at scale.
2. What is an item in DynamoDB?
An item is one record in a DynamoDB table, similar to a row. It is a collection of named attributes and can be up to 400 KB.

Non-key attributes are flexible, so different items can have different attributes. However, the primary key and secondary-index key attributes must follow their defined key schema and scalar key types.
It is the key whose value DynamoDB hashes to determine data placement. It is also used to target items for GetItem or Query access patterns.
5. What makes a good partition key?
High cardinality and evenly distributed access. Avoid keys where a small number of values receive most traffic, because they can create hot partitions.
A sort key is the second part of a composite primary key. Items with the same partition key can have different sort keys and can be queried in sort-key order or ranges.
Query retrieves items for a specific partition-key value and is usually efficient. Scan reads every item or index entry before filtering and becomes expensive as data grows.
8. Does FilterExpression reduce the read cost of a Scan?
No. DynamoDB reads the items first and applies the filter afterward, so a filter reduces returned results but not the data initially read for capacity purposes.

A GSI can use a different partition key and optional sort key, can be added or removed later, scales separately, and supports eventual reads only. An LSI uses the same partition key as the table with a different sort key, must be created with the table, shares throughput, supports strong reads, and has a 10 GB per-partition-key item-collection limit.
10. Can you strongly consistently read from a GSI?
No. GSI reads are eventually consistent only.
A read may temporarily return an older committed value after a recent write. Repeating the read later returns the updated value.
12. What is a strongly consistent read?
A strong read returns the latest committed value reflecting prior successful writes. It is supported on tables and LSIs.

On-demand automatically manages throughput and charges per request; it is the default/recommended option for many workloads. Provisioned mode configures RCUs/WCUs and is useful for steady predictable workloads and specific cost-control cases.

One WCU provides one write per second for an item up to 1 KB.
A partition receiving disproportionate traffic so its per-partition capacity is exhausted even if the table has unused capacity elsewhere. Better key distribution is the main solution.

A write that succeeds only if a condition expression evaluates to true, such as attribute_not_exists(id) or version = 4. It is useful for concurrency control and business invariants.
Store a version number and update only if the current version matches the one read. If another writer changed the item, the conditional update fails instead of silently overwriting it.
Yes. TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems provide ACID transactions for up to 100 unique items and 4 MB total, within the same account and Region.

28. Why does DynamoDB not support JOIN?
It is a distributed NoSQL database optimized for predictable key-based access. Relationships are usually modeled by denormalizing data, composite keys, and access-pattern-specific indexes.
It stores multiple entity types in one table and uses partition/sort key patterns to colocate related data so an access pattern can often be answered with one Query.
A GSI that only includes items containing the index key attributes. This is useful for indexing rare states such as failed jobs without indexing every table item.

For a table with LSIs, the total item collection for one partition-key value, including base-table items and LSI projections, cannot exceed 10 GB.
33. How many GSIs and LSIs can a table have by default?
Up to 20 GSIs by default and up to 5 LSIs.

Store the large object in S3 and store its object key, URL, status, and searchable metadata in DynamoDB.
35. How do you prevent duplicate order creation?
Use a conditional PutItem such as attribute_not_exists(orderId), or use an idempotency key item/transaction depending on the workflow.

Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a fully managed publish-subscribe messaging service. Publishers send a message to a topic, and SNS pushes copies of that message to the topic's subscribers.
SNS is push-based: SNS delivers messages to subscribers rather than subscribers polling the topic.
One publish can fan out to many independent subscribers.
SNS supports application-to-application messaging and application-to-person notifications.
Topics are logical communication channels; subscriptions connect endpoints to a topic.
The SNS mental model: publisher -> topic -> many subscribers.
Fan-out: one event can notify many systems.
Loose coupling: publishers do not need to know how subscribers are implemented.
Event-driven architecture: react to business events such as OrderCreated or PaymentSucceeded.
Notifications: deliver to email, SMS, mobile push, HTTP/S endpoints, Lambda, SQS, and Firehose depending on topic type.
Independent subscribers: failure in one subscriber does not have to block others.
Order Service publishes OrderCreated once. SNS sends a copy to Billing, Email, and Analytics subscribers.
Application or AWS service that publishes messages.
Logical channel that receives published messages.
Connection between a topic and an endpoint.
Destination that receives messages: SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, email, SMS, mobile push, Firehose, etc.
Standard topics support the broadest endpoint types; FIFO topics are specialized for ordered application messaging.
Choose Standard for most pub-sub and human notifications. Choose FIFO only when strict ordering/deduplication across SQS subscribers is a real requirement.
Subscribers should tolerate possible duplicate deliveries.
Standard topics support the broadest range of protocols/endpoints.
If a subscriber needs durable buffering and retry isolation, place an SQS queue between SNS and the application worker.
Make event consumers idempotent when duplicate processing would cause incorrect business effects.
Messages use MessageGroupId for ordered groups.
Messages in the same group preserve order; different groups can progress in parallel.
MessageDeduplicationId or content-based deduplication helps prevent duplicate publishes.
High-throughput FIFO mode can scope deduplication to MessageGroup for greater throughput.
FIFO ordering is maintained within each message group.
SNS FIFO topics do not directly deliver to email, SMS, mobile push, HTTP/S, Firehose, or Lambda. Subscribe an SQS queue, then consume from SQS.
This is one of the most important AWS messaging patterns to know.
Publisher publishes one event to SNS.
SNS sends a copy to each subscribed SQS queue.
Each downstream service processes its own queue independently.
SQS adds durable buffering, consumer-controlled retries, visibility timeout, and queue backlog.
A slow Analytics consumer does not block Billing or Email.
Why not subscribe all workers to one SQS queue?
One SQS queue distributes work among competing consumers. Multiple SQS queues behind SNS give each service its own copy of the event.
Filter policies let subscribers receive only relevant messages.
Without a filter policy, a subscription receives every message published to the topic.
Filter policies are JSON conditions configured on each subscription.
FilterPolicyScope=MessageBody can match fields inside a JSON message body.
Filters reduce unnecessary downstream work and simplify publisher code.
One OrderEvents topic can deliver payment events to Billing, shipment events to Shipping, while Analytics receives everything.
Message attributes are metadata sent alongside the message body.
They are commonly used for filtering, routing hints, content type, event type, tenant ID, or correlation ID.
Keep core business facts in the event body; use attributes for routing/metadata when appropriate.
Raw delivery removes the standard SNS JSON envelope for supported endpoints.
By default, SNS wraps the original message in an SNS JSON notification envelope containing metadata.
Raw message delivery can send the message body directly to SQS, HTTP/S, and Firehose subscriptions.
This is useful when consumers only need the payload and do not want to parse SNS metadata.
Raw delivery is simpler for consumers, but you lose the SNS envelope fields unless you carry needed metadata in the message itself.
SNS uses protocol-specific delivery policies when a subscriber cannot receive a message.
AWS-managed endpoints such as SQS and Lambda have AWS-defined retry behavior.
HTTP/S subscriptions support configurable delivery policies.
Retries use backoff to avoid repeatedly hammering an unavailable endpoint.
If retry attempts are exhausted and a DLQ is configured, SNS sends the undeliverable message to the DLQ.
SNS DLQs capture delivery failures after retry policy is exhausted.
The DLQ must be an Amazon SQS queue.
The DLQ is configured on the subscription, not on the topic.
Each subscriber can have its own DLQ because each endpoint can fail independently.
Monitor DLQ message count with CloudWatch alarms.
Investigate and redrive/reprocess after fixing the cause.
SNS DLQ captures SNS-to-subscriber delivery failures. SQS DLQ captures messages that a consumer repeatedly receives but fails to process.

7. What is the difference between a Standard and FIFO SNS topic?

Standard topics support all SNS endpoint protocols and best-effort ordering. FIFO topics preserve strict ordering per MessageGroupId and provide deduplication features, but delivery is for SQS subscribers.

18. How does SNS retry failed deliveries?

19. Can SNS deliver email and SMS?

20. Does email/SMS make SNS a durable work queue?

21. What is the current SNS message-size limit?

22. How do you secure an SNS topic?
Use least-privilege IAM/topic policies, HTTPS, KMS server-side encryption when needed, and VPC endpoints for private API access where appropriate.
23. How does SNS publish to an SQS queue securely?
The subscription connects SNS to the queue, and the SQS queue resource policy must allow the SNS topic/service to call sqs:SendMessage.
24. Can SNS work across AWS accounts?

25. What is the benefit of filter policies?

SNS is simpler topic-based pub-sub and supports human notification channels. EventBridge is a broader event bus with richer event-pattern routing and many service/SaaS integrations.
27. When should I use SNS instead of direct SQS?
Use SNS when multiple independent subscribers each need their own copy. Use direct SQS when one logical worker pool should process each job.
28. What is FIFO archive and replay?
SNS FIFO topics can archive messages for up to 365 days and replay a selected time range to subscribers for recovery or reprocessing.
29. Can Standard topics replay old messages?
Not with the same built-in FIFO archive/replay feature. A common approach is to archive Standard-topic messages externally, for example through Firehose to S3.
30. How would you troubleshoot a subscriber not receiving messages?
Verify publish success, subscription confirmation, filter policies, IAM/topic/endpoint permissions, delivery status logs/metrics, and the subscription DLQ.
31. What is a common SNS microservices pattern?
Publish business events to SNS, subscribe one SQS queue per downstream service, and let each service process independently.
32. Why should HTTP SNS subscribers be idempotent?
SNS retries failed deliveries, so an endpoint can receive the same notification again. Idempotency avoids duplicate business effects.

Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) is a managed message queue. Producers send messages to a queue, and consumers receive and process those messages later.
SQS helps decouple services so they do not have to be available or equally fast at the same time.
It buffers bursts of work and lets consumers process messages at their own speed.
SQS stores messages durably across multiple Availability Zones.

Load leveling: sudden spikes can wait in the queue instead of overwhelming workers.
Reliability: work is not lost just because a consumer is temporarily unavailable.
Asynchronous processing: user-facing request can finish before background work completes.
Independent scaling: add more consumers when backlog grows.
Retry handling: failed work can be retried and eventually moved to a DLQ.

If successful, consumer calls DeleteMessage using the receipt handle.

However, an application consumer can still see/process a message again if processing fails, the visibility timeout expires, or deletion does not complete.

Choose a timeout longer than the normal processing time.

If timeout is excessively long, failed messages take longer to become available for retry.

2. Why use SQS instead of calling another service directly?

3. What is the difference between a producer and a consumer?

Standard queues provide very high throughput, at-least-once delivery, and best-effort ordering. FIFO queues preserve strict order within a MessageGroupId and provide deduplication/exactly-once processing features.

No. FIFO prevents duplicates being introduced by SQS and provides send deduplication, but application failures or visibility expiration can still lead to reprocessing. Idempotent consumers are still recommended.
In FIFO queues, MessageGroupId identifies an ordered group. Messages in the same group are processed one at a time in strict order, while different groups can be processed in parallel.
It is a FIFO identifier used to recognize duplicate sends. Re-sending the same deduplication ID within the 5-minute deduplication interval does not enqueue another duplicate message.

A DLQ is a separate queue where SQS moves messages that have been received unsuccessfully too many times, based on the source queue redrive policy.

19. What is the SQS message retention period?

20. What is the maximum SQS message size?

23. How does Lambda consume SQS messages?
A Lambda event source mapping polls SQS, batches messages, and invokes the Lambda function. The function itself does not need to implement ReceiveMessage polling.
24. What happens when one SQS message in a Lambda batch fails?
By default the batch can be retried. With partial batch responses, the function can report only failed message IDs so successfully processed messages do not need to be retried.
25. How should Lambda visibility timeout relate to function timeout?
The queue visibility timeout must be at least as long as the function timeout, and in practice should allow enough time for processing and retries.
SQS is a durable work queue consumed by workers. SNS is publish-subscribe fan-out that pushes a published message to multiple subscribers.
SNS can fan out one event to multiple SQS queues. Each downstream service gets its own durable queue and processes independently.
SQS is best for buffering durable work for consumers. EventBridge is an event-routing bus with rich rules and many integrations. They are often used together.
29. How do you scale SQS consumers?
Monitor queue depth and age of oldest message, then scale consumers while respecting downstream capacity. For ECS/EC2, backlog per consumer is a useful signal.
30. How do you prevent duplicate business effects?
Design the consumer to be idempotent using techniques such as unique event IDs, database uniqueness constraints, conditional updates, or a processed-message store.
31. What IAM permissions does a basic SQS consumer need?
Typically sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, and sqs:ChangeMessageVisibility on the target queue. A producer normally needs sqs:SendMessage.
A temporary identifier returned when a message is received. It is used to delete or change visibility for that received copy and changes if the message is received again.

34. Why might FIFO processing be slow?
A hot MessageGroupId can serialize work because only one message from that group is processed at a time. Use multiple meaningful groups when business ordering allows it.
35. When should I choose Standard over FIFO?
Choose Standard for most high-throughput asynchronous work when strict ordering is not required. Choose FIFO only when ordering/deduplication requirements justify it.

Amazon API Gateway is a managed AWS service for creating, publishing, securing, monitoring, and managing HTTP, REST, and WebSocket APIs.
It acts as a front door between API clients and backend services.
Backends can include AWS Lambda, HTTP services, ECS/EC2 applications behind load balancers, and supported AWS services.
API Gateway handles API-management concerns so your backend can focus on business logic.
It scales as request traffic changes; you do not provision API Gateway servers.
The simplest mental model: client -> API Gateway -> backend service.
2. Why Do We Use API Gateway?
Expose a clean public API without exposing backend implementation details.
Route requests to Lambda, containers, EC2 services, or HTTP backends.
Apply authentication/authorization before traffic reaches the application.
Configure throttling and quotas to protect downstream services.
Publish separate stages such as dev, test, and prod.
Use a custom domain such as api.example.com.
Collect access logs and CloudWatch metrics.
Build RESTful APIs or real-time WebSocket APIs.
API Gateway is to APIs what a managed front desk/security/routing layer is to a building: it receives requests, checks rules, routes them, and returns responses.
The first design decision is choosing HTTP API, REST API, or WebSocket API.
API keys, usage plans, caching, request validation, WAF, private API endpoints
Backend can push messages to clients
Use HTTP API when you need a straightforward Lambda/HTTP API and do not need REST API's advanced API-management features. Use REST API when those extra features matter.
WebSocket APIs are different from normal request/response APIs. A connection stays open, so the client and backend can send messages independently.
Useful when the server needs to push data to the client without polling.

2. Why would you use API Gateway in front of Lambda?

It gives the Lambda function an HTTP API endpoint and adds routing, authorization, CORS, throttling, stages, custom domains, and monitoring. Lambda focuses on business logic while API Gateway manages the API layer.
3. What are the three major API Gateway API types?
HTTP API, REST API, and WebSocket API. HTTP and REST APIs use request/response HTTP communication, while WebSocket APIs provide persistent bidirectional communication.
4. HTTP API vs REST API - what is the main difference?

HTTP APIs are simpler and generally lower cost. REST APIs provide more API-management features such as API keys/usage plans, per-client throttling, request validation, caching, WAF integration, and private API endpoints.
5. What is a route in API Gateway?
A route maps an incoming request pattern to an integration. For an HTTP API, an example route is GET /users. In REST APIs, the similar model is resource + method.
The integration is the backend API Gateway invokes after a request matches a route/method. Examples include Lambda, an HTTP endpoint, a VPC Link private backend, or a supported AWS service.
It is an integration where API Gateway sends request information to Lambda in a defined event structure and Lambda returns a proxy-formatted result containing the HTTP status, headers, and body.
A stage is a named environment or reference through which a deployed API is invoked, such as dev, test, or prod. A stage can have its own settings and URL mapping.
A deployment is a point-in-time publishable API configuration. A stage is the named environment/reference that points to a deployment and exposes it to clients.
10. What authorization methods can API Gateway use?
Depending on API type, common options include AWS IAM authorization, JWT/OIDC authorization, Amazon Cognito, and Lambda authorizers for custom rules.
11. Is an API key an authentication mechanism?
No. API keys are primarily used to identify API consumers for REST API usage plans and metering/throttling. Use IAM, JWT/Cognito, or a Lambda authorizer for real authentication/authorization.

REST API usage plans associate API keys with API stages and optionally configure client-specific request throttling and quotas.

A common reason is CORS. Browsers enforce CORS rules while tools such as Postman usually do not.

API Gateway is an API-management service with routes, authorizers, stages, usage plans, and API publishing features. ALB is primarily a Layer-7 load balancer for distributing HTTP/HTTPS traffic across application targets.
22. API Gateway vs Lambda Function URL?

A Lambda Function URL is a simpler direct HTTP endpoint for one Lambda function. API Gateway supports richer routing, authorization choices, API lifecycle, custom domains, multiple backends, throttling, and API-management features.
23. When would you use a WebSocket API?
Use it when you need persistent two-way communication or server push, such as chat, notifications, live dashboards, collaboration, or multiplayer applications.
24. How would you secure a public API?

Use HTTPS, appropriate authorization (IAM/JWT/Cognito/Lambda authorizer), least-privilege backend IAM permissions, throttling, validation, logging/monitoring, and where applicable AWS WAF. Do not rely on API keys alone for security.
25. What would you check if API Gateway returns 502?
Check the backend/integration response format, Lambda errors, permissions, integration configuration, and logs. For Lambda proxy integration, malformed Lambda responses are a common cause.
26. What would you check for 504 Gateway Timeout?

Check backend response time, integration timeout behavior, downstream dependencies, database calls, network paths, and whether the operation should be asynchronous instead of a long synchronous API request.
27. How can API Gateway call a private ECS service?
Create a private integration using a VPC Link, connect the API route to an ALB/NLB or supported service-discovery target, then route traffic to the private ECS tasks.
28. Can API Gateway directly perform business logic?

It can perform API-level routing, transformations, validation, authorization, and some direct AWS service integrations, but complex business logic should normally live in Lambda or application services.
29. How do you monitor API Gateway?
Use CloudWatch metrics and alarms, access logs, REST API execution logs where appropriate, backend logs such as Lambda CloudWatch Logs, and tracing such as X-Ray where supported.
30. Which API type should I choose in a normal serverless interview scenario?

If the requirements are a simple Lambda/HTTP RESTful API, HTTP API is a strong starting point. Choose REST API when requirements explicitly need its advanced features. Choose WebSocket API for persistent bidirectional communication.
